parts.title: Why I put my phone away
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
For years, I read on my phone. It was practical: I always had it with me, and I could read a page while I waited for the bus. But last January, I noticed something strange. I had been 'reading' for hours every day, yet I could not remember the last book that I had finished.

So I made a rule: no phone for the first hour after I got home. Instead, I picked up a paperback that had been on my shelf for two years. The first evening was difficult. I kept reaching for my pocket, and after ten minutes I got up to make tea. But on the third evening, something changed. I read for forty minutes without moving, and I did not want to stop.

Since then, I have read twenty-three books. I do not think that paper is better than a screen, and I still use my phone for news and messages. The difference is that a book has no notifications. Nothing flashes, and nobody sends me a message in the middle of a chapter.

My friends were surprised when I told them. Some said that they would never manage it. I do not blame them, because I would have said the same last year. Now I just lend them a book and say, 'Try it for one evening.'

questions.prompt: Why did the writer first read on her phone?
options: She always had it with her
It cost less than buying books
Her friends told her to do it
questions.explanation: She says it was practical because she always had it with her.

questions.prompt: What problem did she notice in January?
options: She could not remember finishing a book
She was spending too much on books
She no longer enjoyed good stories
questions.explanation: She read for hours but could not remember the last book she had finished.

questions.prompt: How did she feel on the first evening?
options: She enjoyed it from the first minute
She found it hard to stay with the book
She fell asleep after ten minutes
questions.explanation: She kept reaching for her pocket and got up after ten minutes.

questions.prompt: What does she say about paper books and screens?
options: She thinks screens are bad for children
She has stopped using her phone completely
She does not prefer paper to screens
questions.explanation: She says she does not think paper is better and that she still uses her phone for news and messages.

questions.prompt: What does she do when friends say they could not do it?
options: She explains her rule to them again
She tells them to buy a paperback
She offers to lend them a book
questions.explanation: She lends them a book and tells them to try it for one evening.

parts.title: The little library on Alder Street
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
On Alder Street, between a bakery and a bus stop, there is a small wooden box with a glass door. Inside, there are about thirty books. It is a street library, and anyone can borrow a book from it for free. [1] The idea belongs to Maureen Tait, a retired teacher who built the box herself three years ago.

'I got tired of seeing good books in rubbish bins,' she says. [2] Within a week, the shelves were full, and neighbours were leaving notes inside the covers about their favourite stories.

The rules are simple. Take a book, and bring it back when you have finished, or leave a different one instead. [3] Maureen says that this surprised her, because she had expected some books to disappear. 'In three years, the number of books has hardly changed,' she says.

Now street libraries are appearing in other parts of the town. [4] Maureen helped the first two groups to build theirs, and she gives them advice about wood and paint. 'The hardest part is the roof,' she laughs. [5] 'If it leaks, you will have thirty wet books and thirty unhappy readers.'
sentences: Some are run by schools, and others by neighbours or shops.
Nobody has to sign a form or show a card.
The bakery next door sells fresh bread and cakes every morning.
The box must keep the books dry, or the whole idea fails.
Most people follow them, and very few books are ever lost.
So she built a small box, painted it blue and filled it with her own books.

gaps.explanation: The sentence explains that the books are free and that no card is needed, which follows "borrow a book from it for free".
The sentence tells what she did next, and the following sentence says the shelves were full within a week.
The sentence says that most people follow the rules, which Maureen finds surprising because few books disappear.
The sentence explains that the street libraries are run by groups, and the next sentence says she helped the first two groups.
The sentence explains why the roof matters, and Maureen then talks about leaks and wet books.

parts.title: How to read more
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage:
Many people say that they would like to read more, but they do not know where to [1]. The best way to begin is to make reading a daily habit. Choose a quiet time, such as before bed, and read for just ten minutes. If you find a book boring, do not [2] yourself to finish it. There are millions of other books, and you will soon [3] one that you enjoy.

It also helps to carry a book with you [4] you go out, so that you can read on the bus or while you wait for a friend. Finally, try to talk about your books. When you tell a friend about a story, you remember it much [5], and they might want to read it [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: People ask "where to start" when they do not know how to begin.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: We say "force yourself to do something", and the gap is followed by "to".

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: You find a book that you enjoy.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "Whenever you go out" means each time you leave home.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "Much better" is the comparative form after "remember it".

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: At the end of a positive sentence, "too" means "as well".

parts.title: A guide for new members
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Welcome to Greenwood Library! If you have just joined, [1] is a short guide to help you. You can borrow up to ten books at [2] time, and you may keep them for three weeks. If you want to keep a book for longer, you can ask [3] the front desk or renew it online. Anyone who returns books late [4] to pay a small fine of ten pence a day. There is also a quiet room upstairs [5] you can study, and the computers are free to use for one hour. We hope [6] will enjoy your visits.

gaps.explanation: The text introduces the guide with "here is" or "this is".
The fixed phrase is "at a time", meaning on each occasion.
You ask at the front desk.
"Anyone" takes "has to pay" in the present simple.
"Where" introduces the place in which people can study.
The library hopes that you, the reader, will enjoy your visits.

parts.title: The Summer Reading Challenge
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: hannelore
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Summer Reading Challenge at Brookfield Library. My name is Hannelore, and I look after the children's section. The challenge starts on the first of July and finishes at the end of August. Every child who joins receives a free folder, and each time you read a book, you get a sticker for it. If you read six books, you win a medal. We have more than two hundred new books on the shelves this year, including some about space and football. On Saturdays, we also have a reading club at eleven o'clock, where a storyteller reads aloud. It takes place in the garden if the weather is good. To join, you only need to give us your name at the front desk. It is completely free, but you must be a member of the library. Parents are welcome to stay and listen, but please keep the noise down. I hope to see you all soon!

gaps.explanation: The challenge finishes at the end of August.

gaps.explanation: Every child who joins receives a free folder.

gaps.explanation: Hannelore says there are more than two hundred new books.

parts.title: A writer for children
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: My guest today is Lottie Brandt, who writes stories for children. Lottie, when do you write?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: Early in the morning, before my children wake up. The house is quiet, and I have two hours before breakfast.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: Where do your ideas come from?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: Mostly from things that my own children say. My son once told me that his teddy bear had a job, and that became my first book.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: Do you ever have days when you can't write?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: Often! When that happens, I go for a long walk. It's strange, but ideas appear when I stop trying to find them.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: What do children say when you visit schools?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: They ask very direct questions. One boy asked me why my characters were always so naughty. I told him that good characters are boring.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: Is there a book you wish you had written?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: A little story about a lost umbrella that my grandmother used to read to me. It's simple, but I still remember every page.

turns.speaker: philip
turns.text: And what are you working on now?

turns.speaker: lottie
turns.text: A book about a girl who collects shadows. It's nearly finished, but I'm not sure about the ending.
